passages.title: Faith must be tested, not merely claimed
passages.tafsir:
This passage opens Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt by putting a question to anyone who has ever said the words *I believe*: did you imagine the saying of it would be the end of the matter? Ayat 1–7 hold together as a single argument — the claim of faith is examined (2), it has always been examined (3), the one who thinks he can slip away from that examination is deceiving himself (4), and for the one who endures it there is a meeting, a reward, and a mercy that outweighs everything the trial cost him (5–7).

## The letters, and where Ibn Kathir points

Ayah 1 is **Alif Lām Mīm** — three disconnected letters. Ibn Kathir does not restate their meaning here; he simply refers the reader back to what he wrote at the beginning of his commentary on Sūrat al-Baqarah about the letters that open certain sūrahs. He treats the question as settled in its proper place and moves straight to the matter this sūrah has come to press.

## Ayah 2: a question that is really a rebuke

**"Do people think that they will be left alone because they say: 'We believe,' and will not be tested?"**

Ibn Kathir identifies the form precisely: *this is a rebuke in the form of a question*. Arabic often frames a reprimand as a question — not to gather information, but to make the listener hear his own assumption said aloud and recognise how thin it is. Nobody argues in so many words that a verbal profession should exempt him from difficulty. But we live as though it should, and the ayah drags that expectation into the light.

The meaning, says Ibn Kathir, is that **Allah will inevitably test His believing servants according to their level of faith**. Notice the two halves of that: the testing is certain, and it is calibrated. It is not random weather.

**The word: *fitnah*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *lā yuftanūn* — "they will not be put to test" — is derived from *fitnah*, which means trial or test. The grammar is passive, and that is worth pausing on: the ayah does not say that people will not struggle, but that they will not *be put* to the test. Something is done to them, by Someone. The believer is not the agent of his own testing; he is the one tested.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites what he calls an authentic hadith, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that *the people most severely tested are the Prophets, then the righteous, then the next best and the next best; a man will be tested in accordance with the degree of his religious commitment — the stronger his religious commitment, the stronger his test.* (Ibn Kathir does not name the collection at this point, so neither will we.)

This hadith turns the usual intuition upside down. We instinctively read hardship as a sign of divine displeasure, and ease as a sign of approval. The Prophet ﷺ places the Prophets — the most beloved of creation to Allah — at the very top of the list of the afflicted. Severity of trial tracks the *strength of a person's religious commitment*, not his distance from Allah. So when a believer finds his religious life costing him something, the ayah and the hadith together tell him he is not being pushed out of the caravan; he is being moved forward in it.

Ibn Kathir then lines this ayah up with two others that make the same demand. *"Do you think that you will enter Paradise without Allah knowing those of you who fought (in His cause) and knowing those who are the patient?"* (3:142) — and there is a similar ayah in Sūrat at-Tawbah. And: *"Or think you that you will enter Paradise without such (trials) as came to those who passed away before you? They were afflicted with severe poverty and ailments and were so shaken that even the Messenger and those who believed along with him said, 'When (will come) the help of Allah?' Yes! Certainly, the help of Allah is near!"* (2:214).

That last verse records a Messenger and his believers at the end of their endurance, asking aloud when relief will come — and the answer is not a reprimand but a reassurance. Trial is not evidence that the promise has failed.

## The occasion of revelation: the Companions at the hijrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that, **according to many narrations, the background to the revelation of this ayah was the harassment the Companions faced from the disbelievers at the time of the hijrah**. That is the human scene behind the words: people who had said *we believe* and found that the sentence cost them their safety, their homes, and their standing among their own people — and who may well have wondered whether that was how it was supposed to go.

The ayah answers: yes. This is how it goes. And Maʿārif is careful to add, citing Qurtubi, that **although this was the background, the message is common to all times** — the pious, the saints and the scholars will face trials and tribulations in every age. The occasion of revelation explains the verse; it does not confine it.

**The forms trial takes.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays them out plainly. Sometimes trial comes through the enmity of the disbelievers and the sinful, in the form of affliction — as the Prophet ﷺ and many other prophets experienced. Sometimes it comes in the form of disease — as Sayyidnā Ayyūb (peace be upon him) experienced. And for some people several kinds are combined at once. So the reader who is not being persecuted for his faith should not conclude the ayah has nothing to say to him; a sickbed is on the list.

And Maʿārif adds the promise that keeps this from being bleak: the believers, especially the prophets and the pious, pass through many trials in this world — **however, they always come out victors in the end.**

## Ayah 3: "so that Allah will know" — what that can possibly mean

**"And We indeed tested those who were before them, so that Allah will indeed know those who are true, and He will know those who are liars."**

Two things happen in this ayah. First, the precedent: this is not a new policy introduced for the community of Muhammad ﷺ. Every believing community before was put through it. Second, the stated purpose — and here a real question arises, one the classical scholars met head-on. If Allah already knows everything, what does it mean that He tests *so that He will know*?

**Ibn Kathir's answer** is to state the creed first and interpret the phrase second. The purpose, he says, is that *He will make known* which people are sincere in their claim to be believers and which are lying. Then he affirms without qualification: **Allah, glorified and exalted, knows what has happened in the past and what is yet to come, and He knows how that which will not happen would have happened if it were to happen.** That last clause is the strongest statement of the point — His knowledge reaches even to unrealised possibilities. And Ibn Kathir notes that **all the Imams of Ahl as-Sunnah wal-Jamāʿah are agreed on this**; it is not a contested corner of belief.

He then reports the way Ibn ʿAbbās and others read such expressions — for instance *"only that We know"* in 2:143 — as meaning *only to see*. Ibn Kathir explains the distinction: **seeing has to do with what is there, whereas knowledge is broader than seeing, since it includes what is not present as well as what is.** In other words, the ayah is speaking of the point at which the thing is actually there to be seen — not of Allah acquiring information He lacked.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān approaches the same phrase from the human side.** Its point is that testing exists so that the distinction between the good and the bad, the sincere and the insincere, **comes to the surface, so that others should also know**. And it gives a concrete reason why that matters: if the hypocrites remain mixed in among the sincere believers and are never identified, that itself may create a number of problems. A community that cannot tell its true members from its pretenders is a community in danger.

Maʿārif adds a second explanation, which Hakīm ul-Ummah Thānawī (may Allah have mercy on him) takes from his teacher Maulānā Muḥammad Yaʿqūb (may Allah have mercy on him): **sometimes people are addressed by descending to their level of understanding.** The ordinary person distinguishes the sincere from the hypocrite by putting him to the test — that is simply how human beings come to know character. So Allah addresses people in the idiom they think in, and says *We would find out who is sincere and who is not*, **even though He knows everything from the very beginning.** This is a courtesy of speech towards the listener, not a limitation in the Speaker.

Read this way, the ayah is not a puzzle about divine knowledge at all. It is a statement about *realisation*: faith that has never been pressed exists as a claim; faith that has been pressed and held exists as a fact — in the record, in the person, and in the sight of everyone watching.

## Ayah 4: the other audience

**"Or think those who do evil deeds that they can outstrip Us? Evil is that which they judge!"**

Having addressed the one who says *I believe*, the passage turns to the one who does not. Ibn Kathir explains: those who are not believers should not think that they will escape such trials and tests — for ahead of them lies **a greater and more severe punishment**. He glosses *outstrip Us* with a single word: **"escape" from Us**. And *"Evil is that which they judge"* means: what they think is evil — their calculation is a bad calculation.

Placed here, ayah 4 closes off the escape route the previous ayat might have seemed to leave open. If faith brings testing, why not simply stay outside it? Because there is no outside. The disbeliever is not spared the trials of this life, and beyond them stands something far heavier. Nobody outruns Allah. The choice is never between being tested and being left alone; it is between a trial that is followed by reward and a reckoning that is not.

## Ayat 5–7: what the tested believer is being carried towards

After three ayat of pressure, the passage opens out.

**Ayah 5: "Whoever hopes in meeting with Allah, then Allah's term is surely coming, and He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower."** Ibn Kathir reads *the meeting with Allah* as the Hereafter, and reads the one who "hopes" for it as the one who **does righteous deeds and hopes for a great reward with Allah**. Hope here is not wishful thinking; it is hope with work attached. To such a person, Allah will fulfil his hopes and reward him for his deeds in full — and, says Ibn Kathir, **this will undoubtedly come to pass**. The appointed term is not a possibility; it is fixed and on its way.

Then the two names at the end of the ayah, which Ibn Kathir ties directly to that certainty: **He is the One Who hears all supplications, and He knows and understands the needs of all created beings.** For a person in the middle of trial, this is the load-bearing sentence of the passage: the duʿāʾ — the supplication — that you make in the dark is heard, and the need you cannot even articulate is already known.

**Ayah 6: "And whosoever strives, he strives only for himself. Verily, Allah stands not in need of any of the creatures."** Ibn Kathir compares this to *"Whosoever does a righteous good deed, it is for himself"* (41:46). Whoever does a righteous deed, **the benefit of that deed will come back to him** — for Allah has no need of the deeds of His servants. And he presses it as far as it will go: **even if all of them were to be as pious as the most pious man among them, that would not add to His dominion in the slightest.** The ayah's own word for Allah here is *ghaniyy* — free of all need. He is not enriched by our worship and not diminished by our neglect.

This reframes the trial completely. If Allah gains nothing from our striving, then the striving was never a service rendered to a Master who needed it. It was always an investment we were being invited to make in ourselves. The struggle of the tested believer is not a tax levied on him; it is capital deposited to his own account.

**Ayah 7: "Those who believe and do righteous good deeds — surely We shall expiate from them their evil deeds, and We shall indeed reward them according to the best of that which they used to do."** Ibn Kathir draws out the logic: though Allah has no need of His creatures, **He is kind and generous to them**. Two gifts are named. First the erasure: their bad deeds are expiated. Then the reward — and note the wording — measured against **the best of what they did**, not the average of it. Allah takes a servant's finest hour as the standard by which the whole life is paid out.

Ibn Kathir spells out the arithmetic of that generosity: **He will accept the fewest good deeds, and in return for one good deed will give anything between ten rewards and seven hundred; but for every bad deed He will give only one evil merit — or even that He may overlook and forgive.** The scales are deliberately, gloriously uneven. He cites in support: *"Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of a speck of dust, but if there is any good, He doubles it, and gives from Him a great reward"* (4:40).

## A note from the previous sūrah, and from a commentator's own trial

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān arrives at this sūrah having just finished Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ, whose final ayah reads *"Everything is going to perish except His Face"* (28:88). It explains that **"His Face" here means the very Being of Allah** — so the meaning is that everything other than Allah is mortal and will be destroyed and will vanish. It notes that **some commentators** have instead taken "His Face" to mean the good deeds people perform exclusively for Allah, in which case the sense is that such deeds alone escape destruction while all other things perish. Both readings sit naturally at the door of our passage: what survives is Allah, and what survives of us is what was done for Him — which is exactly what ayah 7 promises to preserve and repay.

And there is one more thing in Maʿārif that belongs to this passage more than to any commentary. Its author records that he completed the commentary on Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ on the 9th of Dhū al-Qaʿdah 1391 AH (September 1971), in conditions of war — Karachi bombarded daily for fourteen days, the city severely damaged, hundreds of Muslims martyred, many houses demolished, and the fourteen-day war ending on the sad note that East Pakistan was cut off, with about ninety thousand troops surrendered there and killing still going on. He writes that every Muslim was struck with grief and bewilderment, and then simply says: *"Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we shall return"* — adding that to Him alone is the complaint made, and there is no refuge from Allah except with Him.

A commentator reached the ayat about being tested while living inside a testing he could not explain, and what he had to write was the ayah itself. That is what these seven ayat are for.

## Living it

**Stop reading hardship as a verdict.** The hadith Ibn Kathir cites makes the severity of trial track the strength of a person's religious commitment. Difficulty is not proof that Allah is displeased with you.

**Expect the examination; do not try to schedule it.** Ayah 2 promises testing without specifying its form. Maʿārif's list — affliction at the hands of enemies, disease, or several kinds combined — is broad enough that no one is exempt and no one can predict his own paper.

**Let the trial finish its work.** Per Maʿārif, the point of the test is to bring what is inside a person out onto the surface, so that others should also know. Endurance is how the claim of ayah 2 becomes the truthfulness of ayah 3.

**Make duʿāʾ while it is still dark.** Ayah 5 attaches *All-Hearer, All-Knower* to the promise of the coming term for a reason: He hears all supplications and knows the needs of every creature.

**Do the small good deed anyway.** Ibn Kathir's arithmetic — ten to seven hundred for one good deed, one for one bad, and even that possibly forgiven — means nothing you offer is too small to be worth offering, and no record is too damaged to be worth repairing.

passages.title: Pressure from parents and faith that wavers
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat put a believer's faith under two very different kinds of pressure and watch what happens. In ayah 8 the pressure comes from the people a person loves most — his own parents — pulling him toward shirk. In ayah 10 it comes from others who hurt him for believing. What binds the passage together is the question underneath both: when holding on to Allah becomes expensive, who actually holds on? Ayah 9 answers with the reward of those who do; ayah 11 answers with the exposure of those who do not.

## Ayah 8: the command comes right after Tawhid — and that is deliberate

Ibn Kathir makes a point of the placement. Allah commands His servants to be dutiful to their parents *after* urging them to adhere to belief in His Tawhid, "because a person's parents are the cause of his existence." Allah is the cause of your being at all; your parents are the means through which He brought you into the world. So the claim of Allah is named first, and the claim of parents immediately after it.

Ibn Kathir then spells out what each parent is owed and why: the child must treat them with the utmost kindness and respect — "his father for spending on him and his mother because of her compassion for him." Two different kinds of giving, both creating a real claim.

To show how far that claim reaches, Ibn Kathir brings the passage of Sūrat al-Isrāʾ (17:23–24): "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him. And that you be dutiful to your parents. If one of them or both of them attain old age in your life, say not to them a word of disrespect, nor shout at them, but address them in terms of honor. And lower unto them the wing of submission and humility through mercy, and say: 'My Lord! Bestow on them Your mercy as they did bring me up when I was young.'" That is the standard the Qur'an sets. Ibn Kathir observes that although Allah orders us to show kindness, mercy and respect towards them in return for their previous kindness, He then says: "but if they strive to make you associate with Me, which you have no knowledge of, then obey them not." The duty is affirmed in full — and then one thing is carved out of it.

## The words themselves

**وَصَّيْنَا (waṣṣaynā) — "We have instructed."** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Mazharī, explains that *waṣiyyah* means to call someone for some action *when the call is based on advice and well-wishing*. It is not the cold language of a decree. Allah is counselling man here, for his own good.

**حُسْنًا (ḥusnan) — "good."** Maʿārif notes that *ḥusn* is an infinitive meaning "to be good," and what is meant here is to **adopt good behaviour** toward one's parents. Not a feeling only, and not a single act — a settled manner of dealing. As Maʿārif puts it, the meaning of the sentence is quite clear: Allah has advised man to treat his parents kindly.

**جَاهَدَاكَ (jāhadāka).** Ibn Kathir renders it "if they strive to make you associate with Me"; Maʿārif renders it "if they insist upon you that you should ascribe partners to Me," and speaks of parents who *force* toward infidelity or toward associating someone with Allah. Not a passing suggestion, then — sustained pressure. And what they are pressing him toward is described as something "which you have no knowledge of."

## The occasion of revelation: Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ

This is where the passage comes alive, and both commentaries give it the weight.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reports that the verse was revealed in connection with Sayyidunā Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ (may Allah be pleased with him) — one of the ten Companions to whom the Prophet ﷺ had given the good news of being in Paradise, those called *al-ʿAshrah al-Mubashsharah*. And the detail that makes the story bite: Saʿd was an extremely obedient son to his mother and was always alert to look after her comfort. This was not a rebellious young man looking for a reason to break with his family.

When his mother, Ḥamnah bint Abī Sufyān, learnt that her son had accepted Islam, she got very upset. She warned him against it, and then swore an oath: she would neither eat nor drink unless he turned back to his ancestral religion, or she would die of thirst and hunger, and he would be blamed universally for being the killer of his mother. Maʿārif cites Muslim and Tirmidhī for this, and adds that through this Qur'anic verse Saʿd was commanded not to listen to his mother.

Ibn Kathir gives the report in Saʿd's own voice. In his Tafsīr of this ayah, at-Tirmidhī recorded that Saʿd said, "Four Ayat were revealed concerning me" — and he told his story. He said: "Umm Saʿd said: 'Did Allah not command you to honor your parents? By Allah, I will not eat or drink anything until I die or you renounce Islam.'" Ibn Kathir adds the harrowing detail that when they wanted to feed her, they would force her mouth open. Then this ayah was revealed. Ibn Kathir notes this Hadith was also recorded by Imam Aḥmad, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and an-Nasāʾī, and that at-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

Maʿārif adds, from Baghawī's narration, that Saʿd's mother did not eat and drink for a day and night — and according to some other versions, for three days and three nights — and, sticking to her oath, remained hungry and thirsty.

Feel the position he was in. As Maʿārif puts it, for Saʿd his mother's love and obedience was one thing, but Allah's command was another, which naturally took precedence over everything else. So he went to her and said to her firmly: "Dear mother, if there were hundred spirits in your body, and they were departing one by one, I would not have deserted my religion even seeing that scenario. It is now up to you whether you eat and drink or die. In any case I cannot abandon my religion." Having been disappointed by his firmness, she started eating food.

Notice the shape of his answer. He addresses her as "Dear mother" and refuses her demand in the same breath. That is exactly the shape of ayah 8: the duty of kindness stands, and one thing is carved out of it.

## The limit: obedience has a ceiling

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān states the principle plainly: the limit of kind treatment with parents should not go beyond the point where it comes into conflict with the injunctions of Allah. If they force toward infidelity or toward associating someone with Allah, then they must not be obeyed — as advised in the hadith **لَا طَاعَةَ لِمَخْلُوقٍ فِي مَعْصِيَةِ الْخَالِقِ**, "A created being must not be obeyed in disobedience of the Creator." Maʿārif reports it from Imam Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim, who held it as Ṣaḥīḥ.

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 8 the same way: if they are idolators and they try to make you follow them in their religion, then beware of them, and do not obey them **in that**. The restriction is precise. Not "do not obey them"; "do not obey them in that."

## "Unto Me is your return" — the two things Allah will reward

The end of ayah 8 turns the whole matter over to the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir draws out what will be weighed there: you will be brought back to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, and "Allah will reward you for your kindness towards them **and** your patience in adhering to your religion." Both. The son who held his ground *and* kept honouring his mother is rewarded on two counts, not forgiven for one at the cost of the other.

## Ayah 9: gathered with the righteous, not with your family

Ayah 9 lands as the answer to the loneliness ayah 8 creates: "And for those who believe and do righteous good deeds, surely, We shall make them enter with the righteous."

Ibn Kathir's comment here is the emotional heart of the passage. It is Allah Who will gather you **with the group of the righteous, not with the group of your parents** — "even though you were the closest of people to them in the world." For a person will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection with those whom he loves, and Ibn Kathir specifies the kind of love meant: **religious love**.

So Saʿd, who could not follow his mother's religion, does not lose his belonging. He is gathered into a better company.

## Ayah 10: the man whose faith cannot survive being hurt

Now the passage turns from a believer under pressure to someone who only *looked* like one. Ibn Kathir introduces ayah 10 as Allah mentioning the descriptions of "the liars who falsely claim faith with their lips, while faith is not firm in their hearts."

The diagnosis is exact. When a test or trial comes in this world, they think that **this is a punishment from Allah**, so they leave Islam. That is what the ayah means by "they consider the trial of mankind as Allah's punishment." Ibn ʿAbbās said of this phrase: "Meaning that their trial is leaving Islam if they are made to suffer for Allah." Ibn Kathir notes this was also the view of others among the Salaf.

The wording of the ayah itself marks the confusion: what they suffer is *fitnat an-nās*, the trial of mankind — harm coming at the hands of people — and they treat it as *ʿadhāb Allah*, Allah's punishment. Having read it that way, they leave.

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it the man of Sūrat al-Ḥajj: "And among mankind is he who worships Allah as it were upon the edge: if good befalls him, he is content therewith; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face" — and the passage runs on to "That is a straying far away" (22:11–12). Faith on a ledge. It holds while conditions are pleasant and slides the moment they are not.

## The second face: "We were with you all along"

The same person shows up again when the wind changes. "And if victory comes from your Lord, they will say: 'Verily, we were with you.'" Ibn Kathir explains: if victory comes from your Lord, O Muhammad, and there are spoils of war, these people will say to you, "We were with you" — meaning, we are your brothers in faith.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān traces the whole arc in one line: such people join the infidels when they apprehend some kind of torture from them, but when Allah's help comes to the Muslims in a battle against the infidels, they pretend to be Muslims on the plea that they had joined the infidels only because they feared to be persecuted by them.

Ibn Kathir shows this is a recognised Qur'anic portrait by citing 4:141 — those who wait and watch about you: if you gain a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" But if the disbelievers gain a success, they say to them, "Did we not gain mastery over you and did we not protect you from the believers?" — and 5:52, "Perhaps Allah may bring a victory or a decision according to His will. Then they will become regretful for what they have been keeping as a secret in themselves."

Then the ayah closes the escape route with a question: "Is not Allah Best Aware of what is in the breasts of the creatures?" Ibn Kathir's gloss: does Allah not know best what is in their hearts and what they store secretly within themselves, **even though outwardly they may appear to be in agreement with you?** Maʿārif says the same — they did not believe in Islam with their hearts, and this fact cannot be concealed from Him, because He knows whatever lies in the hearts of the people.

The claim "we were with you" may work on the Muslims. It never reaches past the surface with Allah.

## Ayah 11: why the test exists at all

"And indeed Allah knows those who believe, and verily He knows the hypocrites."

Ibn Kathir explains this in terms of testing: Allah will test the people **with calamities and with times of ease**, so that He may distinguish the believers from the hypocrites — to see who will obey Allah both in times of hardship and of ease, and who will obey Him only when things are going in accordance with their desires.

Note that ease is a test too, not only hardship. The "we were with you" moment in ayah 10 is a man failing the comfortable half of the exam.

Ibn Kathir supports this with 47:31 — "And surely, We shall try you till We test those who strive hard and the patient, and We shall test your facts" — and with what Allah said after the battle of Uḥud, with its trials and tribulations for the Muslims: "Allah will not leave the believers in the state in which you are now, until He distinguishes the wicked from the good" (3:179). Uḥud is where Ibn Kathir anchors the principle in history.

## Living it

**Honour is unconditional; obedience is not.** Ayah 8 does not soften the duty of kindness when parents are hostile to faith — Ibn Kathir has Allah rewarding both the kindness towards them and the patience in adhering to one's religion. The believer refuses the demand, not the parent.

**Refusal can be gentle and still be immovable.** Saʿd's answer was affectionate in address — "Dear mother" — and completely unyielding in substance. That is the model.

**Learn to read hardship rightly.** The failure Ibn ʿAbbās describes begins in the interpretation: harm at the hands of people is the trial of mankind, and to treat it as Allah's punishment is the step that leads out of Islam.

**Expect the sorting.** Ayah 11 tells us that both calamity and ease are how Allah distinguishes the believers from the hypocrites. The question the passage leaves with the reader is Saʿd's question: what would it take, and is there anything at all for which I would let go?

passages.title: The disbelievers' offer to carry your sins
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat record a sales pitch and then demolish it. The disbelievers of Quraysh offer the believers a deal: abandon your faith, come back to our way, and whatever sin that lands you with, we will carry it for you. Allah answers that the offer is a lie — no one will carry another's sins — and then turns the tables: the very people making the offer will carry an extra load on the Day of Resurrection, the load of everyone they misled. What holds the passage together is a single image, that of a burden being carried: an imaginary transfer of burdens in ayah 12, and the real, doubled burden in ayah 13.

## The pressure campaign behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: the disbelievers of Makkah tried every device they could think of to pull the Muslims away from their faith and to hinder the progress of the new religion. Sometimes it was a display of power and wealth; sometimes it was planting doubts in believing minds. Ayah 12 records one such move.

Their argument, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays it out, had two layers stacked on top of each other. First: do not leave the religion of your forefathers out of fear of torment in the Hereafter — because no such thing is going to happen in the first place. Then, as a fallback for anyone not persuaded by that: but suppose your belief about the Hereafter did turn out to be true — fine, we are willing to undertake that we ourselves will bear all the torment on your behalf, and you will not suffer at all.

Ibn Kathir gives the same reading in its plainest form: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to those who had believed and followed the truth, *leave your religion, come back to our religion, follow our way* — and the phrase وَلْنَحْمِلْ خَطَايَاكُمْ *(and let us bear your sins)* means, in his words, "if there is any sin on you, we will bear it and it will be our responsibility." He compares it to something people say to one another all the time: **"Do this, and your sin will be on my shoulders."** That is the everyday human ring of the verse. Somebody urging you into something wrong, waving away your hesitation — *don't worry about it, it's on me.*

**A parallel that exposes the trick.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the last rukūʿ of Sūrat al-Najm, أَفَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي تَوَلَّىٰ ۝ وَأَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ — *"Have you seen the one who turned his back, and gave a little, then stopped"* (53:33–34). Once some disbelievers hoodwinked a naive friend of theirs with exactly this line: give us some money here in this world, and in the Hereafter we will save you by taking your share of the torment upon ourselves. He actually started paying them the amount — and then later stopped. Sūrat al-Najm relates in detail his foolishness and the absurdity of what he did. Read alongside our passage, it shows that this was not an abstract debating point. It was a live piece of Makkan salesmanship, and it had already claimed at least one victim.

## Why the offer is a lie — twice over

Allah's response comes in the same breath as the offer: وَمَا هُم بِحَامِلِينَ مِنْ خَطَايَاهُم مِّن شَيْءٍ إِنَّهُمْ لَكَاذِبُونَ — *"Never will they bear anything of their sins. Surely, they are liars."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same words: *"And they are not (able) to bear the burden of their sins in the least. Indeed they are pure liars."*

Notice that the denial is total. Not a reduced share, not a portion held back for them — **anything of their sins, in the least**. And the verdict lands on the promise itself as much as on the men who made it: they are liars.

Ibn Kathir explains the reason simply: they are liars in their claim that they will bear the sins of others, **for no person will bear the sins of another**. He brings other ayat to establish the principle:

- وَإِن تَدْعُ مُثْقَلَةٌ إِلَىٰ حِمْلِهَا لَا يُحْمَلْ مِنْهُ شَيْءٌ وَلَوْ كَانَ ذَا قُرْبَىٰ — *"and if one heavily laden calls another to bear his load, nothing of it will be lifted even though he be near of kin"* (35:18). Even the nearest of kin — the closest relationship on earth buys you nothing there.
- وَلَا يَسْأَلُ حَمِيمٌ حَمِيمًا ۝ يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ — *"And no friend will ask a friend about his condition, though they shall be made to see one another"* (70:10–11). They will be made to see one another and still not ask. So much for the friends who volunteered to carry your file.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a psychological angle and then a theological one. Psychologically: when these people actually see the severity of the torment in the Hereafter, they would not dare to take upon themselves the share of anyone else — hence their promise is false. The promise was made by men who had never seen what they were promising to absorb. Theologically, drawing on the commentary in Sūrat al-Najm: even if they were ready to take on the torment of others, Allah will not allow it — because it is against the code of justice that someone be made to undergo the punishment for a crime another person committed.

So the offer fails at every level at once. They cannot deliver, they would not want to once they saw it, and it would not be allowed even if they did.

## Ayah 13: the load they will actually carry

Having emptied their promise, ayah 13 tells them what they *will* be carrying: وَلَيَحْمِلُنَّ أَثْقَالَهُمْ وَأَثْقَالًا مَّعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ — *"And verily, they shall bear their own loads, and other loads besides their own."*

The contrast is deliberate and stinging. In ayah 12 they say *"let us bear your sins"* — a light, breezy volunteering, offered as a favour they are choosing to do. Ayah 13 answers with a certainty: *verily, they shall bear.* What they claimed they would carry, they will not; what they never bargained for, they certainly will. The vocabulary shifts too. In ayah 12 the talk is of *khaṭāyā*, sins. In ayah 13 it is *athqāl* — loads, burdens — and the word comes back again and again in one short phrase: أَثْقَالَهُمْ وَأَثْقَالًا مَّعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ. You can feel the sagging under a weight that keeps being added to.

Ibn Kathir explains the second load: those who call others to disbelief and misguidance will, on the Day of Resurrection, bear their own sins *and* the sins of others, because of the people they misguided. And he immediately closes off the obvious misunderstanding — **that will not detract from the burden of those other people in the slightest.** He cites لِّيَحْمِلُوا أَوْزَارَهُمْ كَامِلَةً يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَمِنْ أَوْزَارِ الَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَهُم بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ — *"That they may bear their own burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and also of the burdens of those whom they misled without knowledge"* (16:25). "In full" — the followers pay in full, and the misleaders pay on top. Guilt in the Hereafter is not a fixed quantity being shuffled between accounts; it multiplies.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the same point directly: they will not be able to relieve others by taking upon themselves the recompense for the sins others committed — but their effort to misguide people and drift them away from the righteous path is by itself a big sin, and *that* is what will be loaded upon them in addition to their own. This way they carry their own sins as well as the sin of misguiding others.

**Then the questioning.** The ayah ends وَلَيُسْأَلُنَّ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عَمَّا كَانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ — *"and verily, they shall be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about that which they used to fabricate."* Ibn Kathir glosses it as the lies they used to tell and the falsehood they used to fabricate. There is a fine justice in it: the last word about people who spoke so confidently about the next world is that in the next world they will be questioned about exactly what they said.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir supports ayah 13 with a hadith he reports from the Ṣaḥīḥ: *whoever calls others to true guidance will have a reward like that of those who follow him until the Day of Resurrection, without it detracting from their reward in the slightest; and whoever calls others to misguidance will have a burden of sin like that of those who follow him until the Day of Resurrection, without it detracting from their burden in the slightest.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same teaching from Sayyidunā Abū Hurayrah and Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with them), citing Muslim, Ibn Mājah, and Qurṭubī: anyone inviting people toward righteousness is entitled to the collective blessings of all who act on his advice, with no reduction from their reward; and anyone inviting people toward sin suffers the collective punishment of all who act on his invitation, with no reduction from the punishment of those who committed it. This is the sunnah-commentary on *"other loads besides their own"*: influence is recorded, in both directions, and it keeps accruing.

Ibn Kathir also cites, again from the Ṣaḥīḥ, that no person is killed unlawfully without a share of the guilt falling upon the first son of Adam — because he was the first one to initiate the idea of killing another. A crime committed today still charges rent to the man who began the pattern.

**The wronged will be paid — in deeds.** On the closing words about being questioned, Ibn Kathir brings a report recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim from Abū Umāmah (may Allah be pleased with him): the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conveyed the Message with which he was sent, and then said, *"Beware of injustice."* For Allah will swear an oath on the Day of Resurrection and say, "By My glory and majesty, no injustice will be overlooked today." A voice will call out, "Where is so-and-so the son of so-and-so?" He will be brought forth, followed by his good deeds which appear like mountains, the people gazing at them in wonder, until he stands before the Most Merciful. Then the caller will be commanded to announce: whoever is owed anything by this man, or has been wronged by him, let him come forth. They will gather before the Most Merciful, and the Most Merciful will say, "Settle the matter for My servant." They will ask how. He will say, "Take from his good deeds and give it to them." They will keep taking until there is nothing left — and there will still be people with scores to be settled. Allah will say again, "Settle the matter for My servant." They will say, "He does not have even one good deed left." Allah will say, **"Take from their evil deeds and give them to him."** The Prophet ﷺ then quoted this very ayah — *"And verily, they shall bear their own loads, and other loads besides their own; and verily, they shall be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about that which they used to fabricate."* Ibn Kathir notes a corroborating report in the Ṣaḥīḥ with a different chain of narration: a man comes on the Day of Resurrection with good deeds like mountains, but he had wronged this one, taken the wealth of that one and slandered the honour of another; each of them takes from his good deeds, and when nothing is left of them, it is taken from their evil deeds and placed on him.

Two things are worth sitting with here. First, the mercy in the wording: it is *the Most Merciful* who says "settle the matter for My servant" — the settling of scores is not a lapse in mercy but part of a justice in which, as the oath says, nothing is overlooked. Second, this report shows that "carrying other people's loads" is not one narrow scenario about ringleaders of disbelief. Anyone who wronged another human being can arrive on that day carrying weight that someone else generated.

## Living it

**Never accept the "it's on me" offer, and never make it.** This is the practical core. Whether it comes from a friend, a manager, a relative, or a culture that shrugs and says everyone does it — no one on earth is in a position to underwrite your account with Allah. As Ibn Kathir shows from 35:18, nothing of your load will be lifted even by one near of kin. When the moment of pressure comes, ayah 12 has already told you what such reassurance is worth: *"Surely, they are liars."*

**Take your influence seriously.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the ruling out plainly: *invitation to sin is itself a sin, the punishment of which is the same as that of committing it*, and it comes out quite clearly from this verse that the one who invites others to sin, or helps them in committing it, is as much a criminal as the one who actually commits it. That reframes a lot of ordinary life — what we pass on, host, share, encourage, laugh along with, make normal for our children and our friends. Nothing in these ayat says the follower is excused; 16:25 says he bears his burden *in full*. But the one who opened the door bears it too.

**And take the same principle as an invitation.** The hadith runs both ways with matching wording. The same law of accumulating consequence that terrifies in ayah 13 is, turned around, the most generous arithmetic in the religion: whoever calls to true guidance has a reward like that of everyone who follows him until the Day of Resurrection, without diminishing theirs in the slightest. Whatever weight our influence is going to carry — and these ayat guarantee it will carry some — the choice we still have is which side of the scale it lands on.

passages.title: Noah's long call and the saving Ark
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat compress the entire career of Nuh (peace be upon him) into a single breath: nine and a half centuries among his people, a flood, and a ship. But the passage is not really a history lesson. It is a message of comfort, delivered by Allah to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ at a moment when the believers around him were being worn down by hostility — and the two ayat hold together as one thought: **the longest and most relentlessly opposed mission among the earlier prophets ended with the deniers seized by the Flood and the believers carried to safety.**

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the verses just before this described how the disbelievers kept up their opposition and their afflictions on the Muslims as a matter of routine. Allah answers that not with an argument but with a story. As Maʿārif puts it, the Prophet ﷺ is being consoled by being reminded that this pattern — believers harassed by those who reject faith — has been running for a very long time, and that the earlier prophets never lost hope because of it. The conclusion drawn is plain: *you too should not care about the troubles inflicted by the disbelievers, and should keep firmly performing your prophetic obligations.*

Ayah 14 is the beginning of a long sequence. Maʿārif notes that after Nuh comes Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who passed through his own testing trials — the fire of Namrud, migration from Syria to a howling deserted place, the slaughtering of his son — and within Ibrahim's story there is a brief mention of Lut (peace be upon him) and his people, and then, up to the end of the surah, other prophets and their antagonistic peoples. Every one of these stories, Maʿārif says, was related for the same two purposes: to keep the spirit of the Holy Prophet ﷺ high, and to make the Muslims steadfast in their religion. Read that way, ayat 14–15 are the opening panel of a gallery of endurance.

## Why Nuh is placed first

Maʿārif gives two reasons for the ordering.

**First**, he was the very first prophet who had to confront disbelief and the associating of others with Allah. His is the original case of a man standing against a whole people's rejection of tawḥīd — the oneness of Allah.

**Second**, no other prophet experienced harassment to the extent that he had to put up with from his own people. And the reason for that is itself striking: it was because Allah had given him the exclusive honour of a very long life. His long life was a distinction — and living it out, continuously preaching and teaching, meant enduring all sorts of afflictions from the disbelievers throughout that period, including, as Maʿārif states, drubbing and strangling. Then comes the line that gives the passage its whole force: *despite all these difficulties and tribulations he did not lose heart ever.*

That is the pivot for the reader. The honour and the suffering were not two separate things. The long life that made him singular was the same long life that made him suffer.

## "A thousand years less fifty"

The ayah does not simply say "nine hundred and fifty years." It says **a thousand years, less fifty**. The mind is handed the round, staggering figure of a *thousand* first, and only then has fifty subtracted from it. You feel the weight of the millennium before the correction arrives.

Maʿārif is emphatic on the substance: this life span of nine hundred and fifty years as quoted by the Holy Qurʼān is true, without any element of doubt. It is not a figure of speech or an exaggeration to be softened.

Then Maʿārif records a difference over what exactly the number counts. In certain narrations it is mentioned that this relates to the period of his *preaching and teaching*, and that there are additional periods of his life both before this and after the deluge — and Maʿārif closes that discussion with *wa Allāhu aʿlam*, "and Allah knows best," which is the proper posture for a detail like this.

Ibn Kathir preserves a report along those lines. It was recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Nuh received his mission when he was forty years old, and he stayed among his people for a thousand years less fifty; after the Flood he lived for sixty years until people had increased and spread." On that reckoning the 950 in the ayah is the length of the *mission*, framed by forty years before it and sixty after — and those sixty years after the Flood carry their own quiet significance: he lived long enough to see people increase and spread again.

Note also how plainly the ayah puts his part in it: *he stayed among them*. Nine hundred and fifty years of not leaving.

## What those centuries actually looked like

Ibn Kathir fills in what the ayah leaves implicit. Nuh, peace be upon him, stayed among his people for this long period, **calling them night and day, in secret and openly** — and in spite of all that, they still persisted in their aversion to the truth, turning away from it and disbelieving in him. Only a few of them believed with him.

Sit with that ratio. Every hour was used — night and day. Every register was used — the private word and the public proclamation. Across nine and a half centuries. And the harvest was a few.

This is why the passage is a consolation and not a rebuke. If effort guaranteed results, Nuh's people would all have been believers. Guidance was never in his hands.

## "And the Deluge overtook them while they were wrongdoers"

The end of ayah 14 does two things at once. The Flood *seized* them, took them — and then comes the clause "while they were wrongdoers."

That final clause is the verdict attached to the punishment. The water did not fall on an ambiguous people or on a case that was still open. After 950 years of night-and-day calling, they were seized in a state that Allah Himself names: wrongdoing. The length of the warning is what makes the sentence just. Nobody could say they had not been told.

Ibn Kathir draws the lesson directly for the Prophet ﷺ: the meaning is, *after this long period of time, when the Message and the warning had been of no avail — so, O Muhammad, do not feel sorry because of those among your people who disbelieve in you, and do not grieve for them, for Allah guides whomsoever He wills and leaves astray whomsoever He wills. The matter rests with Him and all things will return to Him.*

He supports this with Allah's words elsewhere: "Truly, those, against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified, will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them" (10:96–97). Some hearts will not be moved by any sign whatsoever; the caller is not failing when that happens.

And then Ibn Kathir turns the consolation into a promise: *know that Allah will help you and support you and cause you to prevail, and He will defeat and humiliate your enemies, and make them the lowest of the low.* Nuh's story is offered not only as company in hardship but as evidence of how such stories end.

## "Then We saved him and the Companions of the Boat"

Note who the actor is throughout both ayat: **We sent**, **We saved**, **We made it a sign**. Nuh called night and day, in secret and openly; the deliverance itself is attributed entirely to Allah.

Ibn Kathir explains "the Companions of the Boat" simply: it means **those who believed in Nuh**, peace be upon him. He adds that this has already been discussed in detail in Surah Hud, and there is no need to repeat it here.

So the people named by their place aboard are identified by Ibn Kathir in terms of faith. They are not listed as a family or a tribe. What the ayah names is the boat; what Ibn Kathir names is belief.

## "And made it a sign for all people"

The last clause of ayah 15 is where Ibn Kathir slows down, because there are two ways of reading what "it" refers to. He gives the meaning as *"We caused that ship to remain"* — and then offers the alternatives.

**View one — the ship itself remained.** Ibn Kathir attributes this to Qatadah: that it remained until the beginning of Islam, on Mount Judi. A physical object left standing as a public witness.

**View two — ships in general are the sign.** The alternative is that the concept of sailing in ships was left as a reminder to mankind of how Allah had saved them from the Flood. On this reading, every hull that floats is a running reminder of Nuh's rescue. Ibn Kathir supports it with two passages: "And an Ayah for them is that We bore their offspring in the laden ship. And We have created for them of the like thereunto, on which they ride… and as an enjoyment for a while" (36:41–44); and "Verily, when the water rose beyond its limits, We carried you in the ship. That We might make it an admonition for you and that it might be retained by the retaining ears" (69:11–12).

**The grammatical observation.** Ibn Kathir then names precisely what is happening in the sentence: this is *a shift from referring to one specific ship to speaking about ships in general*. A single, definite object in the first half of the ayah becomes a general category by the end of it. He shows that the Qurʼān does this elsewhere:

- "And indeed We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and We have made such lamps missiles to drive away the Shayatin (devils)" (67:5). Ibn Kathir comments that the lamps which are used as missiles are not the same lamps as are used to adorn the heaven — the reference has widened from the specific to the class.
- "And indeed We created man out of an extract of clay. Thereafter We made him a *Nutfah* in a safe lodging" (23:12–13) — where the "him" made into a drop is not the same individual created from clay.

He notes there are many other similar examples. For the reader, this is a useful key: a pronoun in the Qurʼān can carry you from one thing to the whole kind of thing it belongs to, and missing that shift can make a verse look like it says something it does not.

Note also the reach of the phrase "for all people." The ark was not made a sign only for Nuh's generation, who were gone. It was made a sign for all people — which includes us.

## Living it

The passage asks a few concrete things of a believer.

**Measure your work by faithfulness, not by results.** Nine hundred and fifty years, night and day, in secret and openly, and only a few believed. Nobody will ever have a worse ratio of effort to visible outcome, and Nuh is not presented as having failed. He is presented first, as the opening example. As Ibn Kathir renders the message: Allah guides whomsoever He wills — the matter rests with Him.

**Do not let hostility set your agenda.** The instruction Maʿārif draws out is that the Prophet ﷺ should not care about the troubles inflicted by the disbelievers and should keep firmly performing his prophetic obligations. The persecution is real; it is simply not a reason to stop.

**Do not lose heart.** Maʿārif's summary of Nuh — beaten, strangled, opposed across an unusually long life, and never once losing heart — is the single sentence to carry away from these two ayat.

**Remember that rescue is Allah's doing.** The believers did not save themselves; *Then We saved him and the Companions of the Boat*. Their part, as Ibn Kathir defines them, was that they believed in Nuh.

**Read the world as a sign.** Whether the sign is the ship preserved on Judi or the sailing of ships as such, the point of "a sign for all people" is that Allah leaves reminders standing for those who will look. As the verse Ibn Kathir quotes says, such an admonition is "retained by the retaining ears" (69:12) — the reminder is there; what differs is who is listening.

passages.title: Abraham calls his people from idols
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat give us the opening words of Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) call to his people: a summons to worship Allah alone, a demolition of the idols they had carved with their own hands, and a warning that denial has a long and well-known history. What holds the passage together is a single line of reasoning — *the One who feeds you is the One who deserves your worship, your fear, your thanks, and your return* — followed in ayah 18 by the reminder that if this reasoning is rejected, the messenger has still done his job.

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the setting. The verses just before this described how the disbelievers kept up their opposition and their persecution of the Muslims as a matter of routine. In response, the Prophet ﷺ is consoled by being shown episodes from the lives of earlier prophets: this harassment of believers by the disbelievers has been going on for a very long time, and those earlier prophets never lost hope because of it. So — the implication runs — do not be troubled by what the disbelievers inflict on you either; keep performing your prophetic duties firmly.

The surah began this sequence with Nuh (peace be upon him). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons for putting him first: he was the very first prophet who had to confront outright disbelief and the association of others with Allah; and no other prophet endured harassment from his own people to the extent that he did, because Allah had honoured him with an exceptionally long life. The Qur'an's figure of nine hundred and fifty years is true beyond any doubt; some narrations say this refers to the span of his preaching and teaching, with further years of his life before it and after the flood — *wallāhu aʿlam*. To live that long, continuously preaching, enduring every kind of affliction — including beating and strangling — and never once to lose heart, was his particular distinction.

Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is the second in the sequence, and he too passed through severe trials: the fire of Namrud, then migration from Syria to a howling, deserted place, then the command to sacrifice his son. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that within Ibrahim's story a brief mention is also made of Lut (peace be upon him) and his people, and that the rest of the surah goes on to other prophets and their hostile nations — all of it told to keep the spirit of the Prophet ﷺ high and to make the Muslims firm in their religion.

That is the frame. When you read ayah 16, you are not only listening to a man arguing with idolaters in the distant past. You are being handed a pattern that a persecuted community in Makkah was meant to recognise as its own.

## Who is speaking — ayah 16

Ibn Kathir introduces the passage by naming Ibrahim with four descriptions: Allah's **servant**, His **Messenger**, His **close friend**, and **the Imam of the monotheists**. Ibn Kathir then sets out what Ibrahim called his people to, and the list is worth slowing down over, because the whole passage is built on it. He called them to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate; to fear Him alone; to seek provision from Him alone, with no partner or associate; and to give thanks to Him alone — for He is the One to whom thanks are owed for blessings that nobody but He can bestow.

Notice that this is not one demand but four, and they are four faces of one thing. Worship, fear, asking, and gratitude all belong in the same direction. Split them — worship Allah but fear something else, or thank Allah but ask someone else — and tawhid has already been broken.

**"Worship Allah, and have taqwa of Him"** (*iʿbudū-llāha wa-ttaqūh*). Ibn Kathir's gloss is compact: *worship Him and fear Him alone, with all sincerity.* Taqwa is a word that gets translated many ways, and Ibn Kathir tells us exactly how to take it here: it is fear of Allah, directed to Him alone, and offered sincerely — that is, for Him, not for anyone else's eyes.

**"That is better for you, if you know."** Ibn Kathir explains: if you do that, you will attain good in this world and in the Hereafter, and you will keep evil away from yourselves in this world and the Hereafter. Note both halves. Tawhid is not presented as a burden with a reward attached at the far end; it is presented as the better deal in both lives — good gained, harm averted, now and later. The conditional clause "if you know" quietly locates the problem: the case is plain enough that anyone who genuinely knows would take it.

## The idols dismantled — ayah 17

Ayah 17 turns from the call to the case against what they had. Allah states, Ibn Kathir says, that the idols they worshipped were not able to do them any harm or any good, and tells them: *"You made up names for them and called them gods, but they are created beings just like you."* That interpretation was reported by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was also the view of Mujahid and as-Suddi.

Sit with that sentence. The idols are not a rival order of being. They are creatures — in the same category as the people bowing to them. The only thing that made them gods was a name, and the name was supplied by the worshippers themselves.

**"And you invent falsehood"** — *wa takhluqūna ifkā*. Here the commentators give a second, more literal reading. Al-Walibi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: *"You invent falsehood" means you carve idols* — which do not have the power to provide for you. Put the two reports side by side and you get the full indictment: they carve the object with their hands and then invent the divinity with their tongues. The whole apparatus, wood and name alike, is their own manufacture.

**"Those whom you worship besides Allah have no power to give you provision."** This is the hinge of Ibrahim's argument. He does not begin with abstractions; he begins with the daily bread. Whatever these idols are, they cannot feed you. So the conclusion follows immediately:

**"So seek from Allah your provision"** — *fabtaghū ʿinda-llāhi r-rizq*. Ibn Kathir says this emphasises the point of asking Allah alone, and he links it to two other verses: "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" (al-Fatihah 1:5), and "My Lord! Build for me, with You, a home in Paradise" (66:11). Both are places where the servant turns to Allah and to no one else — the first for worship and help, the second for the one thing that matters most in the end.

Ibn Kathir then glosses the ayah word by word. *Fabtaghū* — "so seek" — means **ask for**. And *ʿinda-llāhi r-rizq* — "from Allah your provision" — means: do not seek it from anyone or anything other than Him, for no one else possesses the power to do anything.

**"And worship Him, and be grateful to Him."** Ibn Kathir: eat from what He has provided, worship Him alone, and give thanks to Him for the blessings He has given you. The sequence is complete and circular — He provides, you ask Him, you eat, you worship, you thank. Every link points back to the same One.

**"To Him you will be brought back."** Ibn Kathir: this means on the Day of Resurrection, when He will reward or punish each person according to his deeds. Ibrahim ends where every serious argument about how to live has to end. Even if a person could get through this life comfortably on borrowed gods, the return is to Allah, and there the accounting is by deeds.

## Denial has a history — ayah 18

**"And if you deny, then nations before you have denied."** Ibn Kathir reads this as: *you have heard what happened to them by way of punishment for opposing the Messengers.* The ayah does not speak of a few stray individuals but of whole nations, whole communities. Denial on that scale is nothing new, and neither is its outcome; the record is public and the audience already knows it — which is why the argument can simply point at it.

**"And the duty of the Messenger is only to convey plainly"** — *al-balāgh al-mubīn*. Ibn Kathir: all the Messengers have to do is convey the Message as Allah has commanded them. Then he adds the sentence that keeps this from becoming fatalism: Allah guides whoever He wills and leaves astray whoever He wills — so strive to be among the blessed. Guidance is entirely in Allah's hand; that is exactly why the servant's response is effort, not passivity.

### Who is being addressed here?

The commentators genuinely differ over whether ayah 18 is still Ibrahim speaking to his people, or Allah speaking directly to the Prophet ﷺ and the Makkans.

**Qatadah** said of "And if you deny, then nations before you have denied": *"These are words of consolation to His Prophet, peace be upon him."* On this reading — as Ibn Kathir notes, and Ibn Jarir stated the same — the narrative about Ibrahim is interrupted here, and resumes only at ayah 24 with "And nothing was the answer of Ibrahim's people…"

**Ibn Kathir himself leans the other way.** From the context, he says, it appears that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said all of what is in this section, and that here he is establishing proof against his people that the Resurrection will indeed come to pass — the evidence being that the passage closes at ayah 24 with "And nothing was the answer of his people…", which reads as the reply to a speech that has been running continuously. He ends, as the scholars do at such a point, with *"And Allah knows best."*

Both readings are held by serious authorities and neither should be flattened into the other. And notice that the difference does not change what the ayah asks of us — because on Qatadah's reading it consoles the Prophet ﷺ, and on Ibn Kathir's reading Ibrahim's ancient warning lands on Makkan ears as if freshly addressed to them. Either way, the ayah reaches forward.

## Living it

**Check where your requests actually go.** Ibrahim's argument was built on provision, and it still works there. The ayah does not say "believe Allah is the Provider"; it says *ask Him* — and, as Ibn Kathir spells out, do not seek it from anyone or anything else, because no one else possesses the power to do anything. A person can hold correct beliefs about rizq while their anxiety, their scheming, and their hopes are all quietly filed elsewhere.

**Do not skip the thanks.** The ayah puts worship and gratitude together, and Ibn Kathir spells it out plainly: eat from what He has provided, worship Him alone, thank Him for what He has given. Gratitude is not an optional refinement on top of tawhid; it is part of directing everything to the One who alone can bless.

**Weigh it the way ayah 16 weighs it.** "That is better for you" — good in this world and the next, and harm kept away in this world and the next. When obedience feels costly, the ayah is not asking you to ignore the cost; it is telling you that you have mispriced the alternative.

**Convey, and leave the outcome.** For anyone who calls others to Allah — a parent, a friend, a teacher — ayah 18 is a release. The duty is the clear conveying. Results are not part of the assignment; Allah guides whom He wills. And the instruction that follows is not "relax" but "strive to be among the blessed."

**And take the consolation as it was given.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's whole point is that these stories were told to keep the Prophet's ﷺ spirit high and to make the believers steadfast. Nuh preached for a lifetime we can hardly imagine and did not lose heart. Ibrahim came through the fire, the migration, and the command to sacrifice his son. If opposition is what you are meeting, you are standing in a very long line — and the ones ahead of you did not turn back.

passages.title: Origination, resurrection, and no escape
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take one objection — "how could we possibly be brought back to life after we have died?" — and answer it with the plainest evidence there is: you were nothing, and here you are. The passage moves from proof, to invitation, to consequence: ayah 19 argues that the One who began the creation can repeat it; ayah 20 sends the objector out to look at the world with his own eyes; and ayat 21–23 draw out what follows once resurrection is admitted — that everything returns to a Sovereign no one can escape, who shows mercy and punishes as He wills.

## The argument this answers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies exactly who is being spoken to and what their position was. The idolaters of Makkah **did** believe that it is Allah who created the whole universe. Their disbelief was not in a Creator; it was in a second creation. They "deemed it impossible that the people will be resurrected after they once die."

That is what makes the passage's argument so pointed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls their position a fallacy and says plainly why: "It is strange that these infidels do believe that Allah has originated the creation, but they deny His power to do it again, while the latter is easier than the former." They had already conceded the harder claim. Having granted that a universe can be brought out of nothing by Allah, they had no ground left on which to deny that a body already made once can be made again.

Ibn Kathir frames the whole passage as one continuous teaching. He writes that "Allah tells us that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, showed them the proof of life after death, which they denied, **in their souls**." The proof is not in a book or a debate; it is in the person of the one denying it. Ibn Kathir then continues without a break: "Then he taught them to contemplate the visible signs on the horizons and the things that Allah has created…" — and it is that same teaching he carries straight into ayah 20. One argument, in two movements: first look inward, then look outward.

## Ayah 19 — the proof inside you

*"See they not how Allah originates the creation, then repeats it. Verily, that is easy for Allah."*

The question is not asking for information. It is the Qur'an's way of saying: this is in front of you; why are you not looking?

Ibn Kathir spells out the proof "in their souls": "For Allah created them after they had been nothing at all, then they came into existence and became people who could hear and see." Follow that carefully. There was a time when you were not a thing — no matter, no shape, no name. Then you were. Then you were not merely present but *hearing* and *seeing* — endowed with faculties, awareness, a self. Ibn Kathir's conclusion is the whole argument in one sentence: **"The One Who originated this is able to repeat it, it is very easy for Him."**

**"That is easy for Allah."** The word in the ayah is *yasīr* — easy. Ibn Kathir sets a parallel ayah alongside it: "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him" (30:27) — where the word is *ahwan*, "easier."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same comparison out as an argument: "repeating the process of creation is much easier than its origination." That is the hinge on which the deniers' position breaks. They granted the origination and denied the repetition — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that they had it exactly backwards by their own reckoning. The Qur'an meets them on ground they had already conceded, and their objection collapses on it.

## Ayah 20 — go and look

*"Say: 'Travel in the land and see how He originated the creation, and then Allah will bring forth the creation of the Hereafter. Verily, Allah is able to do all things.'"*

Having pointed inward — to the self — the passage now points outward. The ayah opens with a command to convey ("Say"), and what is to be conveyed is itself two commands in sequence: *sīrū*, travel the land, and then *fa-nẓurū*, and look. The evidence is not scarce or specialist; it is spread across the ground, and a person only has to go and stand in front of it.

Ibn Kathir sets out what such a traveller is meant to contemplate — "the visible signs on the horizons and the things that Allah has created: the heavens with their stars and planets, moving and stationary, the earth with its plains and mountains, its valleys, deserts and wildernesses, trees and rivers, fruits and oceans."

What is the traveller supposed to conclude? Ibn Kathir gives the reasoning in two steps. First, all of it "indicates that these are themselves created things" — every one of these magnificent objects is itself made, dependent, brought into being. Second, therefore "there must be a Creator Who does as He chooses, Who merely says to a thing 'Be!' and it is." A world of made things requires a Maker who is not Himself made, and whose making costs Him nothing more than a word.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 20 the same way: it "induced them to look around them to appreciate the splendors of the creation, so that they may apprehend that the One who has originated this marvelous creation can easily repeat the process."

Then the ayah names where this is all going: *"and then Allah will bring forth the creation of the Hereafter."* Ibn Kathir glosses this in a few words — **"meaning, the Day of Resurrection."** The second creation is not a metaphor or a spiritual figure of speech; it is an event on a day. And the ayah seals it: *"Verily, Allah is able to do all things."* The very power they were denying Him is stated outright, without limit.

## Ayah 21 — the Sovereign who is never unjust

*"He punishes whom He wills, and shows mercy to whom He wills; and to Him you will be returned."*

Resurrection established, the passage turns to what resurrection is *for*. Ibn Kathir's comment is a striking statement of Allah's absolute sovereignty: "He is the Ruler Who is in control, Who does as He wishes and judges as He wants, and there is none who can put back His judgement. None can question Him about what He does; rather it is they who will be questioned."

That could be misheard as arbitrariness, so Ibn Kathir immediately closes off that reading in the same breath: "for His is the power to create and to command, and whatever He decides is fair and just, for He is the sovereign who cannot be unjust in the slightest." Two truths are held together, and mainstream Sunni belief holds both without collapsing either: Allah's will is unconstrained by anything outside Him, **and** everything He decrees is perfect justice.

**From the Sunnah.** In support of this, Ibn Kathir cites a hadith he attributes to the Sunan compilers: *"If Allah willed to punish the dwellers of His heavens and His earth, He would do so, while He would not be unjust to them."* Read in the place Ibn Kathir puts it, the hadith is illustrating his point that Allah "cannot be unjust in the slightest" — even in punishment, there would be no wrong done. Mercy, then, is never something owed to a creature.

**"And to Him you will be returned."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is simple: "You will return to Him on the Day of Resurrection." Notice the phrasing of the ayah itself: not "you will go back," but "you will be returned." The returning is not something a person arranges or agrees to; it is done to him. Every soul is going back, the believer and the denier alike; only the reception differs.

## Ayah 22 — nowhere to run, no one to plead

*"And you cannot escape on the earth or in the heaven. And besides Allah you have neither any protector nor any helper."*

The denial is total, and it covers the entire map of existence: not on the earth, not in the heaven. Ibn Kathir states it flatly: "No one in heaven or on earth can flee from Him."

He then gives the reason, and it is worth reading slowly: "for He is the Subduer Who is above His servants, and everything fears Him and is in need of Him, while He is the One Who is Independent of all else." Escape is impossible not merely because Allah's reach is long, but because everything that exists stands in need of Him while He needs nothing at all. You cannot flee to a place that does not depend on Him, in a body that does not depend on Him.

*A note on belief, from me rather than from the commentaries:* when Ibn Kathir says Allah is "above His servants," we affirm that of Him exactly as He has described Himself — real in meaning, without likening it to any created "aboveness" and without explaining it away. That is the way of the Salaf: affirm the attribute, entrust the manner to Him.

Then the second half of the ayah removes the last two exits a frightened person looks for: no **protector** and no **helper** besides Allah. Between the two, the ayah closes the door on both shelter and rescue. In this life people survive judgement through someone's protection or someone's strength; on that Day there is neither, "besides Allah."

## Ayah 23 — the ones who cut themselves off

*"And those who disbelieve in the Ayat of Allah and the meeting with Him, such have no hope of My mercy: and for such there is a painful torment."*

Ibn Kathir identifies exactly who is meant: "Those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and denied the Resurrection." Two denials, and they are precisely the two the passage has been dismantling — the signs (ayah 20's evidence spread across the earth) and the meeting (ayah 21's "to Him you will be returned").

"Such have no hope of My mercy" — Ibn Kathir explains it as: "they will have no share in it." And note the wording of the ayah: *My* mercy. Through the passage Allah has been spoken of as "He" — He punishes, He shows mercy, to Him you will be returned — and here the voice turns direct and personal, at precisely the point where mercy is being withheld. The loss is not from an abstraction. It is from Him.

And the ending: "for such there is a painful torment" — which Ibn Kathir describes as "extremely painful, **in this world and the next**." The consequence is not held entirely in reserve. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the movement of the passage in one line: "After establishing the Resurrection, the last three verses describe the punishment for those who deny it." Proof first, warning after — and the order is not accidental.

## Living it

*What follows is application — my own attempt to carry the commentaries above into daily life.*

**Take the first creation seriously and the second becomes obvious.** The passage's whole method is to make you contemplate what already happened to you. You were nothing. Whenever the Hereafter feels unreal or far-fetched, return to Ibn Kathir's sentence: the One who made you hear and see after you "had been nothing at all" is not going to find your remaking difficult.

**Ayah 20 is a command to go and look.** Travel and observation become worship when the eye is trained on the right thing. A mountain, a river, a coastline, the night sky — Ibn Kathir's list of what to contemplate is an invitation to treat the visible world as evidence, so that it argues you toward faith rather than distracting you from it.

**Live as someone who is on His mercy, not owed it.** If Allah "cannot be unjust in the slightest" even in punishing, then every ease you have is gift, not wages. That is the death of self-satisfaction — and, equally, the death of despair, because a mercy that was never earned can always be given.

**Nothing about you is out of reach.** No place on the earth or in the heaven, no protector, no helper. That is terrifying to the one running from Him, and it is the deepest comfort available to the one running toward Him — because the same total reach that means there is no hiding also means there is nowhere you can fall outside His care.

passages.title: The fire, Lot's belief, and Abraham's migration
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat carry Ibrahim (peace be upon him) from the moment his people ran out of arguments and reached for fire, to the moment Allah rebuilt his life on the far side of it. What holds them together is a single movement: **rejection, rescue, departure, reward.** His people answer him with violence (ayah 24); he answers them with a warning about where their idol-fellowship is heading (ayah 25); he leaves them altogether for the sake of his Lord (ayah 26); and Allah gives him sons, prophethood, scripture, and honour in both worlds (ayah 27). Read together, they speak directly to anyone who fears that obeying Allah will cost them everything.

## Ayah 24 — when the argument is lost, the fire is lit

Ibn Kathir sets the scene precisely. Allah is telling us "how Ibrahim's people stubbornly and arrogantly disbelieved, and how they resisted the truth with falsehood." Ibrahim had just addressed them "with his words of clear guidance" — and their entire reply was two words of violence: **"Kill him or burn him."**

Notice the shape of the ayah: *"the only response of his people was to say…"* Not one counter-argument. Not one defence of their gods. Ibn Kathir puts his finger on exactly why: **"This was because proof had clearly been established against them, so they resorted to using their power and strength."** That is a pattern worth recognising. When a people cannot answer a truth, they attack the person carrying it. Force is what falsehood reaches for when it has run out of reasons — and it is, if you look at it honestly, a confession of defeat.

**The fire itself.** Ibn Kathir fills in the scene from another passage of the Qur'an, where they say, *"Build for him a building and throw him into the blazing fire!"* and Allah comments, *"So they plotted a plot against him, but We made them the lowest"* (37:97–98). They did not do this in a fit of rage; they took their time. Ibn Kathir describes it: they spent a long time gathering a huge amount of firewood, built a fence around it, and set it ablaze "until its flames reached up to the sky." No greater fire, he says, had ever been lit. Then they came to Ibrahim, seized him, put him into a catapult, and threw him in.
