And then: *"Then Allah saved him from the fire."* Ibn Kathir explains the rescue in a single clause — Allah "rescued him from it by making it cool and safe for him." Ibrahim spent several days inside it and emerged unscathed. The greatest fire ever lit, and the tafsir needs one short phrase to account for its undoing.

This is where the closing words land: *"Verily, in this are indeed signs for a people who believe."* The event was there for all of them to see. But note whom the ayah names as the beneficiaries of a sign: *a people who believe*.

**Why this made him an Imam.** Ibn Kathir draws out something worth pausing on. "For this reason and others, Allah made him an Imam for mankind" — and he lists what Ibrahim gave: *he offered himself to the Most Merciful; he offered his body to the flames; he offered his son as a sacrifice; and he gave his wealth to care for his guests.* Body, child, wealth, and self — a whole life handed over, item by item. "For all of these reasons," Ibn Kathir concludes, "he is beloved by the followers of all religions." Leadership in Allah's sight is not claimed; it is paid for.

## Ayah 25 — the friendship that curses you in the end

Having survived their fire, Ibrahim does not go quiet. Ibn Kathir introduces this ayah by saying that Ibrahim "explains to his people that idols are incapable of doing anything," and reads his words as a rebuke for their idol-worship: *"You have taken these as gods and you come together to worship them so that there is friendship and love among you in this world."*

Weigh where Ibn Kathir places the emphasis in that paraphrase. What the idols secure is not power or provision — it is *"friendship and love among you in this world."* The Arabic word in the ayah is **mawaddah**: affection, mutual warmth. So it is worth asking ourselves the question the ayah puts to them: how much of what we hold on to is held because it is true, and how much because letting go of it would cost us the company of the people around us?

Then Ibrahim shows them the expiry date on that warmth: *"but on the Day of Resurrection…"* Ibn Kathir: "the situation will be the opposite, and this love and friendship will turn into hatred and enmity."

- *"you shall deny each other"* — "you will denounce one another and deny whatever was between you."
- *"and curse each other"* — Ibn Kathir specifies the direction it runs: **"the followers will curse their leaders and the leaders will curse their followers."** The cursing goes both ways, up the chain and down it.

He supports this with two other ayat: *"Every time a new nation enters (the Fire), it curses its sister nation (that went before)"* (7:37), and *"Friends on that Day will be foes one to another except those who have Taqwa"* (43:67). That exception is the whole point — the one friendship the ayah exempts is the friendship of those who have **taqwa**, that watchful mindfulness of Allah which makes a person careful of what pleases Him and wary of what displeases Him.

The verse ends without mercy for that path: *"your abode will be the Fire, and you shall have no helper."* Ibn Kathir: "your ultimate destiny after all accounts have been settled, will be the fire of Hell, and you will have no one to help you or save you from the punishment of Allah." And note the quiet symmetry the passage builds — they lit a fire for Ibrahim and it did not touch him; they are walking towards a Fire that the ayah calls their abode. Ibn Kathir closes: "This will be the state of the disbelievers. As for the believers, it will be an entirely different matter" — which is exactly what ayah 27 goes on to show.

## Ayah 26 — one believer, and a road out

*"So Lut believed in him."*

**Who Lut was.** Ibn Kathir reports that it was said he was the son of Ibrahim's brother — Lut ibn Haran ibn Azar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls him Ibrahim's nephew, and adds a moving detail: he was **the very first to accept faith after watching the miracle of Ibrahim in the fire of Namrud.** He saw the flames refuse to burn, and he believed.

**How few they were.** Ibn Kathir states plainly: "None of Ibrahim's people believed in Ibrahim besides Lut and Sarah the wife of Ibrahim." Maʿārif adds that Sarah was Ibrahim's cousin and had accepted the faith. So the believers named to us are three: Ibrahim, Lut, and Sarah — after all that preaching, and after a public miracle.

**A difficulty, and its resolution.** Ibn Kathir raises an honest objection here. How do we square "only Lut and Sarah believed" with the Hadith narrated in the Sahih, in which Ibrahim, passing by a tyrant who asked about Sarah, said "My sister" — and then told her, *"I told him that you are my sister, so do not let him think I am lying, for there are no believers on earth except for you and I, and you are my sister in faith."* If only he and Sarah were believers, where is Lut? Ibn Kathir answers with the humility of a real scholar: "It seems — and Allah knows best — that the meaning here is, there is no other Muslim couple on earth apart from you and I." That is, Ibrahim was speaking of married believers, not of believers absolutely.

Ibn Kathir then traces Lut's later life: he migrated with Ibrahim to Syria, and then, during Ibrahim's lifetime, he was sent as a Messenger to the people of Sadum (Sodom), where he settled.

**Who says "I am emigrating to my Lord"?** The Arabic gives *"and he said"* without naming the speaker, and the scholars differed. Ibn Kathir lays out both possibilities fairly: the pronoun may refer to **Lut**, since he is the last person mentioned before the phrase; or it may refer to **Ibrahim**. He then reports that **Ibn ʿAbbas and Ad-Dahhak** held it to be Ibrahim. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same view from **Ibrahim An-Nakhaʿi and Qatadah**, notes that "some other commentators are of the view" that it was Lut, and then argues for Ibrahim on contextual grounds: the very next sentence, *"And We granted him Ishaq and Yaʿqub,"* points certainly to Ibrahim. As for why Lut is not mentioned again although he travelled too, Maʿārif explains that "being subordinate to him, his separate mention was not called for" — just as Sarah, also travelling with him, is not separately named.

**What hijrah means here.** Ibn Kathir gives the motive in one sentence: Ibrahim "chose to leave them so that he might be able to follow his religion openly." Maʿārif renders his words as *"I am going to leave my homeland towards my Lord,"* and glosses the intention: "he wanted to go to some place where there was no obstacle in worshipping Allah."

Feel the wording: **"I am emigrating *to my Lord*."** Not "to Syria," not "away from these people" — the destination is named as Allah Himself. The geography is incidental; the direction is what matters.

**The route and the age.** Qatadah said: "They migrated together from Kutha, which is on the outskirts of Kufa, and went to Syria." Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, records that **Ibrahim was the first prophet who had to migrate from his hometown for the sake of religion, and that he undertook it at the age of seventy-five.** Seventy-five — an age when a man expects to be settled, not to be starting again in a foreign land. He left his homeland, and the passage records not one word of complaint — only *"I am emigrating to my Lord."*

**"Verily, He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise."** Ibrahim ends his announcement with two of Allah's names, and they are exactly the two a migrant needs. Ibn Kathir explains **al-ʿAzīz** — the All-Mighty: "Power belongs to Him and to His Messenger and to those who believe in him." The men who lit that fire looked powerful; the ayah locates power elsewhere. And **al-Ḥakīm** — the All-Wise: "He is Wise in all that He says and does, and in all His rulings and decrees, both universal and legislative" — that is, wise both in what He decrees to happen in the world and in what He commands us to do. So: the One I am going to is strong enough to protect me, and wise enough that this upheaval is not a mistake. We affirm these names as they came, in the manner of the Salaf — real attributes of Allah, without likening them to anything in creation and without explaining them away.

## Ayah 27 — what Allah gave him back

Everything Ibrahim let go of, Allah returned in a better form. *"And We bestowed on him Ishaq and Yaʿqub."*

Ibn Kathir connects this directly to the leaving, quoting: *"So, when he had turned away from them and from those whom they worshipped besides Allah, We gave him Ishaq and Yaʿqub, and each one of them We made a Prophet"* (19:49). The order in that ayah is the lesson: **first he turned away, then he was given.** As Ibn Kathir puts it, when he left his people, Allah gave him "joy in a righteous son who was also a Prophet, to whom in turn was born, in his grandfather's lifetime, a righteous son who was also a Prophet." Ibn Kathir notes the Qur'an calls Yaʿqub *nāfilah* — "an additional gift" (21:72), a grandson born in his grandfather's lifetime, "who would be a delight to them" (see also 11:71).

**"And We ordained among his offspring prophethood and the Book."** Ibn Kathir calls this "a tremendous blessing," and then spells out just how large it is. Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend and made him an Imam for mankind — and beyond that, **after the time of Ibrahim there was no Prophet who was not from among his descendants.** All the Prophets of the Children of Israel descend from him, from Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim down to the last of them, ʿIsa ibn Maryam — who stood among his people and announced the good news of the Hashimi Qurashi Arab Prophet ﷺ, the last of all the Messengers, the leader of the sons of Adam in this world and the next, whom Allah chose from the heart of the Arab nation, from the descendants of Ismaʿil ibn Ibrahim. Ibn Kathir adds the striking point that from the line of Ismaʿil there is no Prophet besides him ﷺ. One man's willingness to be thrown into a fire opens onto the entire line of revelation, ending with our Prophet ﷺ.

**"And We granted him his reward in this world."** Ibn Kathir: Allah "granted him happiness in this world that was connected to happiness in the Hereafter" — in this world he had plentiful provision, a splendid home, a beautiful and righteous wife, "and he was and still is spoken of highly, for everyone loves him and regards him as a friend." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same observation about his standing: he was made popular and an Imam among the people of the world, respected by all alike — Jews, Christians, and idol worshippers.

Maʿārif draws the general principle out of this phrase: although the real reward for good deeds will be awarded in the Hereafter, **a small part of it is also given in this world.** It notes that some authentic ahadith likewise describe benefits awarded in this world for good deeds, and bad outcomes for evil ones, and that Maulana Hakim-ul-Ummah gathered such reports in his booklet *Jazāʾ ul-Aʿmāl*. So the worldly good a believer sees is a portion, not the payment.

**"And verily, in the Hereafter he is indeed among the righteous."** Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and others explained Ibrahim's standing in one line: **"He obeyed Allah in all ways."** Ibn Kathir links it to *"And of Ibrahim who fulfilled all"* (53:37) — "He did all that he was commanded to do and obeyed his Lord to the utmost" — and to Allah's description of him as *"an Ummah, Qanit to Allah, a Hanif, and he was not one of the idolators… and in the Hereafter he shall be of the righteous"* (16:120–122). Maʿārif adds simply: in the Hereafter he will be among the Salihin, the righteous of Paradise.

## Living it

- **When people cannot answer you, expect pressure, not argument.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 24 — that they turned to force *because* the proof had been established — is a diagnostic tool worth keeping.
- **Audit your loyalties.** Ayah 25 asks a hard question of every group we belong to: is this bond built on something that will still be standing on the Day of Resurrection, or is it a *mawaddah* that will turn to mutual cursing? "Friends on that Day will be foes one to another **except those who have Taqwa**" (43:67).
- **Numbers are not the measure.** Three believers, one of them Ibrahim's own wife. Yet from his line came prophethood, the Book, and — as Ibn Kathir says — every Prophet who came after him. Do not evaluate truth by headcount.
- **Sometimes obedience means leaving.** Ibrahim moved so that he could "follow his religion openly" — so that, in Maʿārif's words, there was "no obstacle in worshipping Allah." The principle scales down: a job, a circle, a habit, a place. And it is never too late; he was seventy-five.
- **Nothing given up for Allah is lost.** Ayah 27 is the receipt. He surrendered his homeland and everything familiar, and received Ishaq, Yaʿqub, prophethood in his line, a good life, and the Hereafter among the righteous — from the One who is *al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥakīm*.

passages.title: Lot rebukes his people's obscenity
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat give us a single scene from the life of the Prophet Lūṭ (Lot), peace be upon him: his open indictment of his people's crimes (ayat 28–29), the answer they threw back at him (the end of ayah 29), and the prayer he turned to Allah with when the argument was over (ayah 30). Charge, contempt, and appeal — that is the shape of the unit, and each part explains the next.

## "And Lūṭ…" — a sentence that leans on what came before

Ayah 28 opens simply: *And Lūṭ, when he said to his people…* — with no verb stated for "And Lūṭ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the verb the sentence is reaching for, marking it as an insertion: *And [ We sent ] Sayyidnā Lūṭ, when he said to his people…* The ayah begins, in other words, with Allah recalling His Prophet, peace be upon him, and drops us straight into what he said.

## The indictment: three named crimes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts the charges precisely: **Lūṭ, peace be upon him, names three vicious sins of his people** — first, the unnatural act of man with man; second, highway robbery against travellers; third, committing sin openly in front of one another in their gatherings.

**The first charge (ayah 28).** "Indeed, you commit **al-fāḥishah** — which Maʿārif renders 'the shameful act' — *which none in all creation has preceded you in.*" Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us how His Prophet Lūṭ, peace be upon him, denounced his people for their evil deed and immoral actions in having intercourse with males, *a deed which none of the sons of Adam had ever committed before them.* That clause is not decoration. The Qur'an is not simply calling the act sinful; it is saying that no one before them had done it — they were the first. Maʿārif adds that of the three sins this first is the most disgusting, never committed before anywhere in the world, and that **even wild beasts abstain from it**; and it reports that the entire ummah is unanimous that it is a worse sin than adultery (*Rūḥ*).

Notice too how ayah 28 states the charge and ayah 29 then *asks* it: **a-innakum la-taʾtūna al-rijāl** — "Do you really lust after other men…?" The rebuke is put to their faces as a question they have to answer for themselves.

**The second charge (ayah 29): wa-taqṭaʿūna al-sabīl.** Our translation renders it "abuse the travellers"; Ibn Kathir's rendering is "rob the wayfarer." Ibn Kathir fills in what that meant in practice: **they would lie in wait on the road, kill people and loot their possessions.** So this was not a private vice tucked behind doors. A whole way of life had formed around preying on strangers — whoever passed through was fair game. Maʿārif calls it plainly highway robbery against travellers.

**The third charge (ayah 29): wa-taʾtūna fī nādīkum al-munkar** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "And practice Al-Munkar in your meetings." Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase: *in your gatherings you do and say things that are not befitting — and you do not denounce one another for doing such things.* Read that second half again. Two evils are named at once: the wrong done in public, and the silence of everyone sitting there while it is done.

## What exactly did they do in their gatherings?

Here the sources are careful and honest. Maʿārif notes that **the Qur'an does not specify the third sin** — it names the venue and the category, not the act. The commentators offered what they had:

- **Mujahid** said they used to have intercourse with one another in public.
- **ʿĀʾishah**, may Allah be pleased with her, and **al-Qāsim** said they used to compete in passing gas and laughing.
- Others said they used to make rams fight one another, or organise cockfights.

Ibn Kathir's verdict on the whole list is striking: **they used to do all of these things, and they were even eviler than that.** Maʿārif adds that some of the Imams of tafsir listed such deeds, including throwing stones at travellers and making fun of them — which, Maʿārif says, **Umm Hānī**, may Allah be pleased with her, reports in a hadith; and that other commentators simply say these insolent people were in the habit of committing sins openly before everyone.

Notice what that list contains: an obscenity, a piece of crude buffoonery, and animal-baiting for entertainment. The range is the point. It was not only that the worst thing was done in the open; the whole tone of public life had sunk. Nothing was too coarse to do in front of your neighbours, and nobody's face changed when it happened.

## The principle Maʿārif draws out: sin done openly is doubled

Because the Qur'an leaves the third sin unspecified, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives a general rule from it, and it is the most portable lesson in the passage: **every sin which is a sin in its own right, if it is committed openly and with indifference, becomes a double sin — whatever type of sin it is.**

There is the wrong itself, and then there is the *flaunting* of it. Joined to it is Ibn Kathir's other half — *you do not denounce one another*. A gathering where wrong is done and no conscience stirs has stopped being a gathering of sound hearts. That is the state Lūṭ, peace be upon him, was standing against, alone.

## Their answer (end of ayah 29)

*"But his people gave no answer except that they said: 'Bring Allah's torment upon us if you are one of the truthful.'"*

The Qur'an's phrasing — **fa-mā kāna jawāba qawmihi illā an qālū**, "their answer was nothing except that they said" — closes off every other possibility. Not a defence, not an excuse, not a plea for time.

Ibn Kathir reads the reply for exactly what it is: **this is indicative of their disbelief, their scornful attitude and their stubbornness.** And observe how the demand is built. They do not deny that punishment exists; they *dare* it to come, and they hang it on his honesty — "if you are one of the truthful." Ibn Kathir notes that alongside these deeds they also disbelieved in Allah and rejected and opposed His Messenger. So this is mockery from people who had heard the warning and treated the warning itself as the joke.

## His prayer (ayah 30)

*Lūṭ, peace be upon him, prayed: "My Lord! Help me against the people of corruption."*

Ibn Kathir's framing is exact — because they answered him like that, **Allah's Prophet asked for help against them.** When speech had done all it could do, he turned from arguing with them to asking his Lord. Two things in that short prayer are worth sitting with.

**"unṣurnī."** Our translation gives "Help me"; Ibn Kathir's gives "Give me victory." The request keeps the matter where it belongs: the outcome is Allah's to give, and the prophet's part, peace be upon him, is to ask Him for it.

**"al-mufsidīn" — rendered "the people of corruption," and by Ibn Kathir "the people who are corrupt."** He does not close by listing the three crimes again. He describes his people by what they had become, and leaves them with Allah.

## Living it

**Say that the wrong thing is wrong, even when you are outnumbered.** Lūṭ, peace be upon him, spoke plainly, in public, to men who then invited a torment on themselves rather than hear him. He did not soften the charge or wait for a friendlier audience.

**Guard your gatherings.** Ibn Kathir's gloss turns the sitting room into a place of accountability: what is said and done there, and what goes unchallenged there, both count. The complaint in ayah 29 is against a *nādī* — a meeting, in Ibn Kathir's rendering — where wrong was done and nobody denounced it.

**Do not make a spectacle of sin.** Maʿārif's rule is a mercy as much as a warning: a wrong done privately is one wrong; the same wrong paraded openly and with indifference is two.

**When argument ends, prayer begins.** Ayah 30 teaches the believer's exit from a losing confrontation: not despair, but *Rabbi unṣurnī* — turning to Allah and asking Him for the help and the victory. Lūṭ, peace be upon him, took his helplessness to the only place where it counted for something.

passages.title: The angels' errand to Abraham and Lot
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat bring the story of Lut (peace be upon him) to its conclusion. A delegation of angels travels first to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) carrying good news, and then on to Lut's town carrying a sentence of destruction. What holds the passage together is one thread running through both halves: **before Allah's punishment falls, His knowledge sorts the people out one by one, and His mercy carries the believers to safety.** Notice that almost the same sentence is spoken twice — "we shall save him and his family, except his wife" — once to Ibrahim in ayah 32 and once to Lut in ayah 33. That repetition is not padding. It is the spine of the passage.

## Why the angels came in the first place

Ibn Kathir opens with the detail that makes the whole scene intelligible: **Lut had prayed.** He asked Allah to help him against his people — and Allah sent angels to help him. So the guests who knock on his door in ayah 33 are not an accident of the road. They are his own duʿāʼ, arriving in human form.

The angels take the long way round. Before reaching Lut, they come to Ibrahim in the form of guests, and Ibn Kathir says he "offered them hospitality in the appropriate manner" — meaning he did for these strangers exactly what a generous man does, without knowing who they were. Then the moment turns. In Ibn Kathir's words, "when he saw that they had no interest in the food, he felt some mistrust of them and was fearful of them." The angels began to calm him down, and gave him the news of a righteous son to be born to his wife Sarah, who was present and was astonished by this. Ibn Kathir notes that he has already explained this scene in his commentary on Sūrat Hūd and Sūrat al-Ḥijr.

This is what ayah 31 calls **al-bushrā**, "the good news." And the order of events is worth noticing. The angels announce a birth before they announce a destruction. Mercy is delivered first.

## Ibrahim speaks up for a doomed town (ayah 31)

Then comes the second half of their errand: "Verily, we are going to destroy the people of this town; truly, its people have been wrongdoers."

Ibrahim's response is the astonishing part. Ibn Kathir writes that when they told him they had been sent to destroy the people of Lut, **"he began to speak up for them, hoping to win more time for them so that they might be guided by Allah."**

Sit with that. He was not defending what they did; he was asking for a delay, on the chance that a delay might turn into guidance. This is the temperament of a prophet: the ruin of even the worst people is not something he wants, because as long as they are alive, guidance is still possible.

## "We know better who is there" (ayah 32)

Ibrahim then names the one thing that most concerns him — "**But there is Lut in it!**" — and the angels answer: "We know better who is there."

The answer is a gentle correction. Ibrahim is anxious that a righteous man might be swept up in a general destruction, as though the punishment were a blind force. The reply tells him that nothing about this is blind. The One who ordered it knows exactly who is inside those walls. And the angels do not stop at reassurance; they give a promise: "**We will verily, save him and his family.**" Ibrahim's worry is answered with a commitment, not a probability.

Then comes the exception, and it is a hard one: "**except his wife, she will be of those who remain behind.**" Ibn Kathir explains the phrase plainly — *of those who remain behind* means **one of those who will be destroyed** — and he gives the reason: "because she used to support them in their disbelief and wrongdoing."

This is one of the Qur'an's most sobering principles, and it is stated twice for emphasis (in ayah 32 to Ibrahim, in ayah 33 to Lut himself). **Being married to a prophet saved her from nothing.** Proximity to righteous people is not righteousness. What counted against her was where her loyalty actually lay — with the wrongdoers, not with the man who shared her house. Rescue in these ayat follows belief and allegiance, not an address or a family name.

## Lut's worst night (ayah 33)

Now the angels leave Ibrahim and arrive at Lut's door. Ibn Kathir says they visited him **in the form of handsome young men**, and when he saw them like that he "was grieved because of them, and felt straitened on their account."

Ibn Kathir spells out the trap exactly:

> he was worried since if he had them as guests then he was afraid for them and what his people might do to them, but if he did not host them, he was still afraid of what might happen to them.

Both doors were shut. Take them in, and he feared what his townsmen would do to them. Turn them away, and he still feared for them. And Ibn Kathir adds the line that makes it truly agonising: **"At that point he did not know who they were."** Lut has no idea that the figures in front of him are the very help he had prayed for. He is standing inside the answer to his own duʿāʼ and cannot see it.

Then the angels speak: "**Have no fear, and do not grieve!**" Both burdens are lifted in the same breath, and both are lifted by the same news: "Truly, we shall save you and your family except your wife: she will be of those who remain behind."

There is a mercy of ordering here too, just as with Ibrahim: **Lut is told he is safe before he is told the town is finished.**

## The punishment from the sky (ayah 34)

Ayah 34 states the sentence: "we are about to bring down on the people of this town a **rijz** from the sky, because they have been rebellious." *Rijz* is rendered in our sources as a great torment, a punishment sent down from heaven — and the ayah gives the reason for it in a single clause: their rebelliousness.

Ibn Kathir then describes what happened: **Jibril (peace be upon him) uprooted their town from the depths of the earth, lifted it up to the sky, then threw it upside down upon them.** On top of that, Allah rained upon them what He describes elsewhere as "stones of Sijjīl, in a well-arranged manner one after another. Marked from your Lord" (Hūd 11:82–83) — and Ibn Kathir quotes with those verses the warning attached to them: "and they are not ever far from the evil doers."

The place where they had lived, he says, Allah turned into **a putrid, stinking lake**, which will remain as a lesson to mankind until the Day of Resurrection. And the punishment does not stop at the edge of this world: Ibn Kathir states that they will be **among those who are most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection**.

## The sign that was left standing (ayah 35)

"And indeed We have left thereof an evident Ayah for a folk who understand."

Ibn Kathir glosses *āyatan bayyinah* simply as "a clear sign," and links the ayah to Allah's words about the same ruins in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt: "Verily, you pass by them in the morning and at night; will you not then reflect?" (37:137–138).

That comparison is the key to the ayah. In the verse Ibn Kathir cites, the people being addressed are told that they themselves **go past these ruins morning and night** — and are then asked whether they will not use their minds. The sign was fully public and constantly in view. That is why ayah 35 reserves its benefit for **"a folk who understand"** (*yaʿqilūn*). The evidence was never the scarce thing. Minds willing to draw the conclusion were.

## A note from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān

Commenting on this passage, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān looks back to Lut's own words to his people earlier in the sūrah and counts **three** sins there: the unnatural offence of man with man; highway robbery against travellers; and committing sin openly before others in their gatherings. Of the three, it says the first is the most disgusting — never committed before in the whole world, something even wild beasts abstain from — and that the entire ummah is unanimous that it is a worse sin than adultery (citing *Rūḥ*).

From the third item Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a principle worth carrying away. Because the Qur'an does not specify which sins they committed openly, it deduces that **any sin, whatever its type, if committed openly and with indifference, becomes a double sin.** There is the wrong itself, and then there is the brazenness.

## Living it

**Pray, then watch for the answer in ordinary clothes.** Lut's rescue arrived at his door as what looked like more danger, and he grieved over the very thing Allah had sent to save him. When relief is on its way, it does not always announce itself.

**Speak up for people rather than gloat over them.** Ibrahim's first move on hearing of a doomed people was to ask for more time for them, hoping they might yet be guided by Allah. Wanting guidance for people whose behaviour disgusts you is prophetic character.

**Never let closeness to good people stand in for your own faith.** Lut's wife lived in a prophet's house and remained behind with the town, because she used to support its people in their disbelief and wrongdoing.

**Guard against the brazenness, not only the sin.** On Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, doing wrong openly and with indifference doubles it. Whatever a person is struggling with, at the very least let them keep the shame that stops it becoming a public display.

**Use your reason on what you already pass every day.** Allah left the sign standing, and ayah 35 says it benefits *a folk who understand*. Ruins, histories, warnings — none of them work on a mind that refuses to think.

passages.title: Midian, 'Ad, Thamud, Pharaoh and Korah destroyed
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These five ayat close the surah's long procession of ruined nations. One prophet's mission is told in miniature — Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to Midian (ayat 36–37) — and then the roll call widens to sweep up 'Ad, Thamud, Qarun, Fir'awn and Haman (ayat 38–39), before ayah 40 gathers every one of them into a single verdict: each was seized for his own sin, by a punishment shaped to fit it, and Allah wronged none of them.

What holds the passage together is not simply that these peoples were destroyed. It is the **anatomy of their ruin**: a messenger came with clarity, they had the sight to see, Shaytan made their conduct look attractive to them, they weighed the world and preferred it — and then a wind, a shout, the ground and the water each took a turn. The passage moves from one story, to a list, to a law.

## A prophet's call, and a town's answer (ayat 36–37)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us how His servant and Messenger Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, warned his people — the people of Madyan — and commanded them **to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate**, and to fear the wrath and punishment of Allah on the Day of Resurrection.

Notice the order of his call. The very first thing out of his mouth is not the commercial fraud his people were famous for. It is *"O my people! Worship Allah."* Sound belief comes first; conduct follows from it. Only after that does he say **"and hope for the Last Day."**

**"Hope for the Last Day" — a phrase worth pausing on.** Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Jarir on it: *"Some of them said that this meant: Fear the Last Day."* So the same expression reaches in both directions — the believer's forward-looking hope and his sober fear of that Day are two faces of one attitude. Ibn Kathir links it to Allah's words elsewhere: *"for those who look forward to (meeting with) Allah and the Last Day"* (60:6). A heart that genuinely expects to stand before Allah is a heart that both longs and trembles.

**"And commit no mischief on the earth as mischief-makers."** Ibn Kathir reads this as forbidding them to make mischief on earth by *spreading corruption*, which he defines with striking plainness: **"going around doing evil to people."** Not a private failing — a mobile, outward-facing harm.

What did that look like in Midian? Ibn Kathir names it: **they used to cheat in weights and measures, and ambush people on the road** — and this, he stresses, was *in addition to* their disbelief in Allah and His Messenger. Two kinds of theft, one open and one disguised: robbery on the highway, and robbery behind the counter. A man who shaves the scale is doing what the bandit does, only politely. And behind both sits the disbelief that made them think no one was keeping accounts.

Then the answer came. Ibn Kathir describes it as a compound punishment: **a mighty earthquake that convulsed their land, and the Ṣayḥah** — the Shout — **"which tore their hearts from their bodies," and the torment of the Day of Shade, when their souls were taken.** He calls it *the torment of a great day*.

The ayah says they became, in their dwellings, *jāthimīn* — the word rendered "prostrate," a body fallen still where it dropped. The early scholars read the image two ways. Ibn Kathir reports **Qatadah: "They were dead."** Others said **they were thrown on top of one another**. Either way the picture is the same: a whole town frozen mid-life.

Note also the grim symmetry, which is the first hint of the law ayah 40 will state outright. They ambushed people *on the road*; the punishment found them **in their own dwellings** — the one place a man assumes he is safe.

Ibn Kathir adds that their story has already been examined in detail in Sūrat al-A'rāf, Sūrat Hūd and Sūrat ash-Shu'arā'. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same observation about the whole group of stories here: they are given only in brief, because the accounts of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and of 'Ad and Thamud have been related in detail in Sūrahs al-A'rāf and Hūd, and the events of Qārūn, Hāmān and Pharaoh have just passed in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ. The point here is not narrative; it is the pattern.

## The roll call widens (ayat 38–39)

Ibn Kathir opens this stretch by telling us it is about **these nations who disbelieved in their Messengers, and how Allah destroyed them and sent various kinds of punishments and vengeance upon them** — and he grounds each one, first geographically and then in terms of what made it formidable.

**'Ad**, the people of Hud, peace be upon him, lived in **al-Aḥqāf — the curved sand-hills — near Ḥaḍramawt in the Yemen**. **Thamud**, the people of Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him, lived in **al-Ḥijr, near Wādī al-Qurā**. And then the sentence that turns history into evidence: **"The Arabs used to know their dwelling place very well, and they often used to pass by it."**

That is why the ayah can say *"their destruction is clearly apparent to you from their ruined dwellings."* This was not a legend from a distant continent or a lost age. The site was known, and the people being addressed went past it. The Qur'an is saying, in effect: you do not need to take My word for it — you have seen it.

The same passage names the three individuals and what each of them had. **Qārūn was the owner of great wealth and had the keys to immense treasures.** **Fir'awn was the king of Egypt at the time of Mūsā**, peace be upon him, and **Hāmān was his minister** — the two of them Copts who disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Wealth, sovereignty, and the administrative machinery that serves sovereignty: between them they cover the great engines of arrogance.

**"Shaytan made their deeds fair-seeming to them, and turned them away from the path."** This is the mechanism of ruin named directly, and it sits in the middle of the list for a reason. Nobody in these nations decided to be a villain. Their conduct was *decorated* for them until it looked reasonable, even admirable — and it was that beautification that pushed them off the road.

### "Though they were intelligent" — *wa kānū mustabṣirīn*

This is the phrase Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up most fully, and it is the sharpest lesson in the passage.

The word, it explains, **is derived from *istibṣār*, which means sight; and *mustabṣir* is used for an observer.** These were not blind men. So the meaning is: **those who insisted on infidelity and shirk (associating a partner with Allah) and got themselves involved in perdition and Allah's wrath were no fools or insane. They were very clever, having insight — but their intelligence and sagacity was confined to mundane considerations.**

Then comes the diagnosis. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says **they did not realise that there would be a day of reckoning for all good and bad actions, when there would be complete justice** — and it points to why that thought should have occurred to them: **the cruel and the oppressors move about in this world without hindrance, but those oppressed and afflicted are compelled to endure injustice. The day this injustice will finish and justice will be the order of the day is called the Hereafter.** That is the one conclusion their sharp minds could not reach; as it puts it, **they are at a loss to comprehend this bit.**

It cites the same theme from the sūrah that follows: **"They know what is superficial of the worldly life, but of the Hereafter they are negligent"** (30:7).

**A second view.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that *some commentators* understood *mustabṣirīn* differently: **that these people did have faith in their heart and did understand well the necessity of the Day of Judgment, but the mundane considerations had compelled them to reject it.** On this reading their tragedy is not a blind spot but a bargain — they saw and sold anyway.

Both readings should unsettle a modern reader more than a story about earthquakes does. The people described here were, by the Qur'an's own testimony, observant and shrewd. Cleverness is not protection. Sight aimed only at what is in front of you will build you a very comfortable road to ruin.

And the same holds for the second half of the list. *"And indeed Musa came to them with clear signs, but they were arrogant in the land — yet they could not outstrip Us."* Fir'awn and Hāmān were not short of evidence; Mūsā, peace be upon him, brought them *clear signs*. Neither seeing nor evidence was what any of these people lacked.

That closing phrase is the hinge of the whole passage. *They could not outstrip Us* — they could not get ahead of Allah, could not outrun Him, could not put themselves beyond His reach. Everything that made them formidable — treasure, throne, apparatus — bought them exactly no distance. Which is what ayah 40 now demonstrates, case by case.

## The verdict: punishments cut to fit the crime (ayah 40)

*"So We punished each for his sins."*

Ibn Kathir's comment on this is five words long, and it is the key to the entire ayah: **"their punishments fit their crimes."** What follows is not a list of disasters; it is a list of *answers*. Read each one against what the people had said or done.

**1. The Ḥāṣib — the stone-carrying wind: 'Ad.** Ibn Kathir explains that this happened **because they said: "Who is stronger than us?"** So there came upon them **a violent, intensely cold wind, which was very strong and carried pebbles which it threw upon them. It carried them through the air, lifting a man up to the sky and then hurling him headlong to the ground, so that his head split and he was left as a body without a head, like uprooted stems of date palms.** They boasted of strength and were answered by moving air — the one thing you cannot fight, cannot see, cannot bribe.

**2. The Ṣayḥah — the Shout: Thamud.** Ibn Kathir notes that **evidence was established against them because of the she-camel who came forth when the rock was split, exactly as they had asked for.** They named the sign; they got the sign. **Yet despite that they did not believe; rather they persisted in their evil behaviour and disbelief, and threatened to expel Allah's Prophet Ṣāliḥ**, peace be upon him, **and the believers with him, or to stone them. So the Ṣayḥah struck them, taking away their powers of speech and movement.** They raised their voices in threats against a prophet, and the Shout took their power of speech away entirely.

**3. Being swallowed by the earth: Qārūn.** Ibn Kathir describes him: **he transgressed, he was evil and arrogant. He disobeyed his Lord, the Most High, and paraded through the land in a boastful manner, filled with self-admiration, thinking that he was better than others. He showed off as he walked** — so **Allah caused the earth to swallow him and his house, and he will continue sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection.** He strutted *on* the earth, so the earth took him *in*. And his punishment is the only one here that is still in motion: the sinking has not stopped.

**4. Drowning: Fir'awn, Hāmān and their troops.** Ibn Kathir: **all of whom were drowned in a single morning, not one of them escaped.** A throne, a minister and an army, and the whole apparatus was gone before the morning was out.

Four crimes, four punishments fitted to them, drawn from four different quarters of creation — wind, sound, earth, water. The Qur'an is showing that the whole of creation stands ready to be summoned as an instrument, and that Allah's justice is not generic. It is precise.

### "It was not Allah Who wronged them"

The ayah ends by shutting off the one objection a reader might still be holding. Ibn Kathir glosses it plainly: **"It was not Allah Who wronged them"** — in what He did to them — **"but they wronged themselves"**: what happened to them was **a punishment for what they did with their own hands.**

This is the moral centre of the passage. Every one of these people had a messenger. Every one of them was given time. The destruction was not an arbitrary act visited on the unlucky; it was the return of their own deed to their own address. *Ẓulm* — wrongdoing — in this ayah does not travel downward from the heavens. It travels outward from the self and comes back.

## Living it

**Take the ruins seriously.** Ayah 38 turns wreckage into an argument because the people addressed *knew the site and often passed by it*. The equivalent for us is not tourism but attention: the collapse of the arrogant is on public record in every generation, and the Qur'an expects us to draw the inference rather than scroll past it.

**Watch for beautification, not just for sin.** Ayah 38 says Shaytan *made their deeds fair-seeming* to them. The dangerous moment is rarely the one where you know you are doing wrong. It is the one where the wrong has acquired a good name.

**Check where your sight is pointed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of *mustabṣirīn* is a warning aimed squarely at capable people: insight confined to worldly considerations is precisely what destroyed them. The question is not "am I clever?" but "does my cleverness ever get applied to the reckoning?"

**Midian's two sins are still available.** Cheating in weights and measures and ambushing people on the road are, in modern dress, the manipulated invoice and the exploited stranger. Ibn Kathir's definition of corruption is worth keeping in the pocket: *going around doing evil to people.*

**And nobody outstrips Allah.** Ayah 39's *"yet they could not outstrip Us"* is addressed to whatever we imagine is our security — wealth like Qārūn's, position like Fir'awn's, competence like Hāmān's. None of it buys a single step of distance. The only sane response is the one Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, opened with in ayah 36: *worship Allah, and look ahead to the Last Day.*
